questions.title: What is web accessibility and why is it an engineering requirement?
questions.quick: Web accessibility means building sites so people with visual, hearing, motor and cognitive disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate and interact with them, including through assistive technology. I treat it as a non-functional requirement, like security or performance, not a visual polish step. In practice that means WCAG-based standards, semantic HTML, keyboard support, sufficient contrast, accessible forms, reusable accessible components, and both automated and manual testing, so quality holds across teams and releases.
questions.revision: Accessibility means everyone, including assistive-technology users, can perceive, understand, navigate and operate the site. It is a built-in quality requirement, enforced by standards, components and testing, not a late fix.
questions.detailed:
Web accessibility (often abbreviated a11y) is the practice of designing and building web content so that people with a wide range of abilities can use it. That includes people who are blind or have low vision, are deaf or hard of hearing, have motor or dexterity limitations, or have cognitive and learning differences. It also helps people with temporary or situational limits, such as a broken arm, bright sunlight or a noisy room.

## Why it is more than a UI concern

Accessibility is determined by markup, component behavior, content, design tokens, state management and release process, so it is an architectural quality attribute. Treating it as a final visual review means defects are found late and expensive to fix.

Consider an example global automotive website. The whole customer journey has to work: browsing vehicle pages, viewing images, comparing trims, searching for a dealer, submitting an enquiry form and using interactive widgets such as sliders, filters and dialogs. A failure at any step can block a user completely.

## What a solid approach contains

- **Standards**: target WCAG 2.2 Level AA unless law or contract requires otherwise.
- **Semantics first**: native HTML elements for structure and controls.
- **Interaction**: full keyboard operability, visible focus, sensible focus management.
- **Perception**: adequate contrast, text alternatives, resizable text.
- **Forms**: labels, instructions and error messages exposed programmatically.
- **Reusable components**: an accessible design system so fixes scale.
- **Testing**: automated checks, manual keyboard testing, screen-reader testing, real user feedback.
- **Governance**: ownership, defect severity and release criteria.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking accessibility only concerns blind users.
- Relying on an overlay or a single scanner score as proof of compliance.
- Fixing issues page by page rather than in shared components.

Legal and contractual requirements vary by region, so the exact obligation should be confirmed with the organization's compliance team, but the engineering practice is the same.

questions.title: What is WCAG and what does POUR stand for?
questions.quick: WCAG is the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, published by the W3C Web Accessibility Initiative. It is the internationally recognized, testable standard for accessible web content. Its guidelines are organized under four principles, POUR. Perceivable: users can perceive the information, for example text alternatives and contrast. Operable: users can operate it, for example keyboard access and visible focus. Understandable: content and behavior are clear, for example labels and error messages. Robust: it works with browsers and assistive technology through correct roles and states.
questions.revision: WCAG is the W3C's testable accessibility standard. POUR: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust. Each guideline has success criteria at levels A, AA or AAA.
questions.detailed:
**WCAG** (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) is a W3C technical standard. The current widely referenced version is 2.2, which is backward compatible with 2.1 and 2.0 in the sense that a page conforming to 2.2 also meets the earlier versions' criteria, apart from the removal of one obsolete criterion (4.1.1 Parsing). It is structured as principles, guidelines and **success criteria**. Success criteria are the testable statements that you are audited against.

## The four POUR principles

| Principle | Question it answers | Typical examples |
|---|---|---|
| Perceivable | Can users sense the content? | Alt text, captions, contrast, text resize, not relying on color alone |
| Operable | Can users operate the controls? | Keyboard access, no traps, visible focus, enough time, target size, dragging alternatives |
| Understandable | Can users understand content and behavior? | Page language, clear labels, consistent navigation, helpful error messages |
| Robust | Does it work with current and future user agents? | Correct names, roles and states, valid use of ARIA, status messages |

## How it is organized

Each principle contains guidelines, and each guideline contains success criteria that carry a conformance level (A, AA or AAA). For example, the contrast criterion sits under Perceivable, and the keyboard criterion under Operable.

## Related W3C materials

- **Understanding WCAG** explains the intent of each criterion.
- **Techniques** (sufficient and advisory) show ways to meet criteria.
- **ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG)** documents keyboard and ARIA patterns for widgets. It is guidance, not part of WCAG.

## Interview tip

Use POUR as a mental checklist for any component: can it be perceived, operated, understood and parsed by assistive tech? Naming one concrete example per letter shows you can apply it rather than recite it.
followUps: Which WCAG version would you target and why?
Where does the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide fit relative to WCAG?
Give one failure example for each POUR principle.

questions.title: What is the difference between WCAG Levels A, AA and AAA?
questions.quick: Each WCAG success criterion is assigned a level. Level A is the minimum, covering barriers that would block access entirely. Level AA adds criteria that address the most common remaining barriers, such as 4.5:1 text contrast, and it is the usual enterprise and legal target. Level AAA is the strictest, and the W3C notes that full AAA conformance is not recommended as a blanket policy because some content cannot satisfy it. Conformance to a level means meeting all criteria at that level and below, so AA includes A.
questions.revision: A is the minimum, AA is the common practical and legal target and includes A, AAA is stricter and often only partly achievable. Conformance is cumulative.
questions.detailed:
WCAG levels are **cumulative**: to claim AA conformance a page must satisfy every Level A and Level AA success criterion. You cannot skip A and meet AA.

| Level | Intent | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| A | Removes barriers that would make content unusable for some groups | Text alternatives for images, keyboard operability, no keyboard traps, page titles |
| AA | Addresses the most common and significant barriers while remaining achievable for most sites | 4.5:1 text contrast, 3:1 non-text contrast, visible focus, resize text to 200%, minimum target size, focus not obscured |
| AAA | Highest level of accessibility, with criteria that are sometimes not feasible for all content | 7:1 enhanced contrast, sign-language interpretation, reading-level requirements |

## Why AA is the common target

Many procurement rules and accessibility regulations reference WCAG 2.x Level AA, though the exact requirement depends on jurisdiction, sector and contract, so confirm it with legal or compliance rather than assuming. AA is demanding enough to remove major barriers and practical enough to apply across a large site.

## What about AAA?

The W3C explicitly says it does not recommend requiring AAA conformance for entire sites, since some content cannot meet every AAA criterion. A sensible approach is to adopt selected AAA criteria where they are cheap and valuable, such as a larger target size on primary calls to action or stronger contrast for body text.

## Conformance details

- Conformance applies to full pages and complete processes. A checkout flow must conform end to end.
- Only accessibility-supported technologies may be relied on.
- Non-conforming content cannot interfere with the rest of the page, for example by trapping focus.

## Common mistakes

- Saying "AA compliant" based on an automated score alone.
- Confusing levels with severity. A Level AA failure can be a critical blocker for a user.
followUps: Why can't AAA be required for every page?
Does an AA claim apply to the whole site or per page?
Which AAA criteria might you adopt voluntarily?

questions.title: Which WCAG 2.2 requirements should every architect know?
questions.quick: Key AA requirements I remember: text contrast of at least 4.5:1, or 3:1 for large text; 3:1 contrast for UI components and meaningful graphics; everything operable by keyboard; a visible focus indicator; focused elements not entirely hidden by sticky headers or banners, which is new in 2.2; pointer targets of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, with exceptions; a single-pointer alternative to dragging; text alternatives for informative images; and programmatic labels and names for every control.
questions.revision: Know contrast 4.5:1, 3:1 for large text and non-text, keyboard, visible focus, focus not obscured, 24 by 24 target size, dragging alternatives, alt text, and labels.
questions.detailed:
This is a quick map of high-value criteria. Names and numbers help in an interview, but understanding the intent matters more.

| Area | Requirement (typical AA unless noted) | SC |
|---|---|---|
| Text contrast | 4.5:1 normal text, 3:1 large text | 1.4.3 |
| Non-text contrast | 3:1 for UI component boundaries/states and meaningful graphics | 1.4.11 |
| Text alternatives | Informative images have equivalent text, decorative ones are ignored | 1.1.1 (A) |
| Keyboard | All functionality operable via keyboard, no traps | 2.1.1, 2.1.2 (A) |
| Focus visible | Keyboard focus indicator is visible | 2.4.7 |
| Focus not obscured | A focused item is not entirely hidden by author content such as sticky bars (new in 2.2) | 2.4.11 |
| Target size | Pointer targets at least 24 by 24 CSS px unless an exception applies (new in 2.2) | 2.5.8 |
| Dragging movements | Provide a single-pointer alternative to dragging (new in 2.2) | 2.5.7 |
| Labels and names | Controls have labels and accessible names; visible label text is part of the name | 3.3.2, 4.1.2, 2.5.3 |
| Reflow and resize | Usable at 200% text size and at 320 CSS px width without two-dimensional scrolling | 1.4.4, 1.4.10 |

## Other new 2.2 criteria worth mentioning

- **Redundant Entry (A)**: do not make users re-enter information already provided in the same process.
- **Accessible Authentication (Minimum, AA)**: do not require a cognitive function test, such as memorizing or transcribing a password, without an alternative or aid. Allow paste and password managers.
- **Consistent Help (A)**: help mechanisms appear in the same relative place.

## Note on removed criteria

WCAG 2.2 removed 4.1.1 Parsing because modern browsers and assistive technology handle it.

## Source clarification

Focus Appearance (2.4.13) is Level AAA in the final 2.2 recommendation, so it is not part of an AA target, although a strong focus indicator is still good practice.

questions.title: What are the WCAG contrast requirements and how do you apply them?
questions.quick: At AA, normal text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background, and large text needs 3:1. Large means roughly 24 CSS pixels regular, or about 18.66 pixels bold. Non-text elements such as input borders, icons and focus rings that are needed to identify a control or its state need 3:1 against adjacent colors. I check ratios with a tool across all states, including hover, disabled-looking and focus, and never rely on color alone to convey meaning.
questions.revision: Text 4.5:1, large text 3:1, meaningful UI components and graphics 3:1. Measure with a tool across all states, and never use color alone for meaning.
questions.detailed:
WCAG expresses contrast as a ratio between the relative luminance of two colors, from 1:1 (identical) to 21:1 (black on white).

## Thresholds

| Content | AA minimum | AAA |
|---|---|---|
| Normal text | 4.5:1 | 7:1 |
| Large text (about 18pt, or 14pt bold, i.e. roughly 24px or 18.66px bold) | 3:1 | 4.5:1 |
| UI components and graphical objects needed to understand content | 3:1 | none |
| Logos, and purely decorative or disabled controls | exempt | exempt |

The 3:1 non-text rule (1.4.11) covers things like the border of a text input if the border is the only visual cue of the field, an icon-only button's glyph, chart lines, and the focus indicator against its surroundings.

## Practical application

- Define color tokens in the design system and document the approved text and background pairings, so that engineers do not pick colors ad hoc.
- Test every state: default, hover, active, focus, selected, error, and text on images or gradients (check the worst point).
- Test in dark mode and high-contrast or forced-colors modes. In forced-colors mode do not strip borders or outlines that become the only visible cue.
- Information must not depend on color alone (1.4.1). An error field needs a text message or icon, not only a red border.

## Quick check in code

```css
.btn-primary {
  background: #0b5cad;  /* example value; verify ratio with a checker */
  color: #ffffff;
}
.btn-primary:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #1a1a1a; /* needs 3:1 against adjacent colors */
  outline-offset: 2px;
}
```

## Common mistakes

- Placeholder text that is too light and used as the only label.
- Judging by eye on a high-quality monitor.
- Assuming a brand color pairing passes without measuring, and forgetting that antialiasing or opacity changes the effective color.

questions.title: What is semantic HTML and why prefer native elements to div-based controls?
questions.quick: Semantic HTML uses elements that express their purpose, such as header, nav, main, button, a, form and label. Browsers and assistive technology use that meaning to expose roles, names and states, and native controls come with keyboard behavior and focus for free. A div with a click handler has none of that. It is not focusable, has no role, and does not respond to Enter or Space. So I use a real button for actions and an anchor for navigation, and only add ARIA when native HTML cannot express the need.
questions.revision: Native elements carry role, name, state, focusability and keyboard behavior for free. A clickable div has none, so use button for actions and a for navigation.

questions.title: What is ARIA and when should you use it?
questions.quick: ARIA, Accessible Rich Internet Applications, is a set of attributes that communicate roles, names, states and properties to assistive technology. The first rule is to use native HTML when it can do the job, because ARIA only changes what is announced. It adds no behavior, so it does not make an element focusable or handle keys. I use ARIA for custom widgets that HTML cannot express, like tabs or comboboxes, and for dynamic state such as aria-expanded, aria-live and aria-describedby, then implement the keyboard behavior myself.
questions.revision: ARIA changes the accessibility tree, not behavior. Prefer native HTML; use ARIA for roles and states HTML lacks, and always implement keyboard support yourself.
questions.detailed:
**ARIA** supplements HTML by describing semantics that the browser cannot infer. questions.title: What is an accessible name and how is it computed?
questions.quick: The accessible name is the text that assistive technology uses to identify a control, such as "Close dialog" for a button. The browser computes it from sources in priority order: aria-labelledby, then aria-label, then native sources such as a label element, alt text, the element's own content, or title as a last resort. Each interactive element needs one, and for controls with visible text the name should include that visible text. I verify it in the browser's accessibility tree rather than guessing.
questions.revision: The accessible name is what a screen reader announces for a control. It comes from aria-labelledby, aria-label, then native sources like label, alt or content. Inspect the accessibility tree.
questions.detailed: The **accessible name** answers "what is this control called?" for screen readers, voice control and other tools.
